draft.title: Covalent bonding
card: A covalent bond forms when two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons. Each atom is held to the shared pair, so the atoms stay joined.
Molecular

small groups of atoms joined by covalent bonds. The bonds inside each molecule are strong, but the molecules are only weakly attracted to each other. Little energy is needed to separate them, so melting points are low.
Network
a huge three-dimensional web of atoms, all joined by covalent bonds. Diamond is one. Melting means breaking many strong bonds, so network solids are very hard and have very high melting points.
Covalent substances have no ions, so they have no charged particles free to move in the way that ions do in a melted ionic compound.
draft.remember: Covalent bonds share electron pairs. Molecules separate easily, but a network must break bonds.

a.q: Which pair of atoms is most likely to join by a covalent bond?
opts: Two non-metal atoms, such as carbon and oxygen
A metal atom and a non-metal atom, such as sodium and chlorine
Two atoms that each give away all their outer electrons
An atom that loses electrons and an atom that gains them
a.why: A covalent bond forms when two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons. The metal and non-metal pairing is tempting, but it involves transfer of electrons to form ions, not sharing.
a.clue: Look for the pair that shares electrons.

b.q: Wax is made of small covalent molecules and melts at a low temperature. Quartz is a covalent network solid and melts at a very high temperature. Why do they differ?
opts: Melting wax separates molecules, but quartz needs bonds broken
Wax has no covalent bonds, but quartz has many of them
Quartz contains ions that wax does not have
The covalent bonds in wax are weaker than those in quartz
b.why: Melting wax only separates molecules that are weakly attracted to each other. Melting quartz means breaking covalent bonds throughout the network. The last option is tempting, but wax has strong covalent bonds inside its molecules. They just do not need to break when it melts.
b.clue: Ask what must be pulled apart when each one melts.

problems.detail: The network bullet says "Melting means breaking many strong bonds, so network solids are very hard". Hardness comes from strong bonds throughout the structure, not from what melting involves. The 'so' gives students a muddled cause.

The distractor "The covalent bonds in wax are weaker than those in quartz" is literally true: Si–O bonds are stronger than C–C and C–H bonds. It is wrong only as an explanation. Rewording it (for example, "Wax melts because its covalent bonds break easily") would make it plainly false.

The last bullet leaves students thinking covalent substances cannot carry charge. Graphite, a covalent network covered in the allotropes point, conducts through delocalised electrons. The hedge "in the way that ions do" is easy to miss.

check.summary: Both answers are sound. In (b), one distractor (wax's covalent bonds are weaker than quartz's) is literally true and should be reworded so only one option is right. The card also links hardness to melting in a muddled way, and its last bullet can suggest covalent substances never conduct, which graphite contradicts.
